title: API Versioning Strategies
learning_outcomes: Explain how api versioning strategies affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from uri path versioning to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on api versioning strategies in api versioning and lifecycle management. You will connect uri path versioning to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: API Versioning Strategies matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying uri path versioning deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Lesson 180 concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: Lesson 180: URI path versioning → Query-parameter versioning → Header and media-type versioning → Trade-offs between approaches.
content_blocks.caption: Follow the 4 syllabus topics in order, then inspect the example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: API evolution must preserve supported consumers or provide an explicit deprecation and migration path. In this lesson, treat “API Versioning Strategies” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: API Versioning Strategies
content_blocks.code:
/v1/orders/ord_123
/v2/orders/ord_123

# Example migration note:
# v1 deprecated on 2027-06-01; clients should move to v2.
# Publish actual dates only after usage and support policies are reviewed.
content_blocks.expected_output: A version strategy communicates the contract boundary; deprecation needs a timeline, consumer evidence, and migration documentation.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “URI path versioning”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Query-parameter versioning” and “Trade-offs between approaches”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Compatibility is a consumer property; deprecations need evidence, communication, and a migration path. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating api versioning strategies. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “URI path versioning” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for API Versioning Strategies with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating api versioning strategies as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: API evolution must preserve supported consumers or provide an explicit deprecation and migration path. In this lesson, treat “API Versioning Strategies” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
Next, connect this idea to Lesson 181: Backward-Compatible Changes.
